opus-5.5.text:
I don't think so, or at least I don't think it's a prerequisite. People often argue that because a child learns to pick up a cup after a handful of tries, a model has to learn the same way before it can be useful in the physical world. That's the wrong frame. The models we build don't learn like humans. They learn from enormous amounts of data through pre-training and then reinforcement learning, and that process has a lot of advantages the human brain doesn't. It's less sample-efficient, but we can throw far more experience at it, run it in parallel, and copy the result instantly.

With robotics, I think the bottleneck has been more practical than conceptual. There just hasn't been an internet-scale corpus of physical interaction data the way there is for text and code. But that's starting to change through simulation, teleoperation, video, and the fact that once you have a decently capable system in the world, it generates its own data. The same scaling dynamics we've seen elsewhere seem to show up there too. You get smooth improvements as you add compute and data, and generalization emerges that nobody explicitly designed for.

Better sample efficiency or continual learning would certainly help, and it's an interesting research direction. But I'd put it in the "nice to have that accelerates things" bucket, not the "fundamental barrier" bucket. My guess is that we'll get very capable robotic control mostly through the paradigm we already have. It may also turn out, as has happened repeatedly, that the thing people said required human-like learning just falls out of scale. Separately, I think the hardware side, meaning actuators, cost, and manufacturing, may end up being as much of a rate limiter as the intelligence side.

fable-5.1.text:
I don't think so, and I'd actually push back on the framing a little, because "human-like learning" smuggles in two separate claims. One is about the data: humans learn to move by being embodied in the world, getting feedback from their own bodies, and nobody hands a toddler a curated dataset. The other is about the algorithm: the brain does something continuous, online, sample-efficient, and we might think you need that to get dexterity.

On the first, I think the lesson of the last five or six years is that the substrate matters much less than people assumed. Language models didn't learn language the way children do. They read the whole internet, which is a wildly unnatural way to acquire a language, and yet they ended up with something that behaves a lot like understanding. My prior is that robotics is going to go the same way. The bottleneck has been data, not some missing ingredient of human cognition. You just can't scrape a trillion tokens of "what it feels like to pick up a cup." But that's an engineering problem. You get it from teleoperation, from simulation, from video, from fleets of robots that are good enough to be deployed and then improve from deployment. Once the data flywheel exists, I expect the same scaling behavior.

On the second, the algorithmic point, I'm more agnostic but still skeptical that we need to copy the brain. Humans are the existence proof that general intelligence is possible with this amount of compute and this amount of experience. They're not the existence proof that it's the only way. We already have models that learn in context, that can take a few demonstrations and generalize. That's not the same as a child learning to walk, but it doesn't have to be. The question is whether it's good enough, and I think the honest answer is we'll find out empirically, probably within a couple of years.

Where I would concede something to the human-learning camp is on the physical world being unforgiving in a way that text isn't. If a language model is wrong, it just produces a wrong sentence. If a robot is wrong, it breaks a plate or hurts someone. So you can't have the same sloppy sample-inefficient loop in the real world that you can on a GPU. That probably means more simulation and more careful deployment, and that's a place where you might borrow ideas about how biological systems stay safe while learning. But that's an argument from caution, not an argument that there's some secret in the brain that we have to replicate.

The thing I'd really watch is that robotics tends to lag the cognitive side by a few years, mostly for data reasons and because hardware is slower than software. I wouldn't read that lag as evidence that something fundamental is missing. I'd read it as evidence that we haven't put the pieces together yet.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think they necessarily do. There’s a distinction between saying that human learning is evidence that a certain approach can work and saying that it’s the only approach that can work. Humans learn robotics, so to speak, with relatively little explicit instruction, but we also come with a lot of structure from evolution. It’s hard to make a clean comparison of sample efficiency.

The question I’d ask is: what’s the bottleneck? Is it understanding the world and figuring out what to do, or is it getting enough experience with the consequences of physical actions? A language model can know a lot about how to assemble something without having the motor skills to do it. You need some way to close that gap, whether that’s demonstrations, simulation, or interaction with the real world.

My guess is that you can get quite far by combining a broadly capable model with training on those interactions. You may need new methods, but I wouldn’t assume they have to resemble how a child learns. The physical world makes collecting experience slower and more expensive, and that could be a bigger constraint than whether we’ve reproduced the human learning process.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think they necessarily need to learn in the same way humans do. You have to distinguish between acquiring a capability and acquiring it with the same amount of experience that a human has. A robot might need much more data than a person to learn a task, but if you can generate that data cheaply in simulation, that may be a perfectly good way to get there.

The interesting question is how much transfers. Can learning from video, from language, and from simulated environments give you representations that make learning in the physical world much more efficient? Or do you need a huge amount of actual interaction with the world? I’m uncertain about that. But I wouldn’t assume that because humans learn robotics one way, that’s the only path to the capability.
